message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) are both placental mammals, but they belong to different orders—Carnivora for lions and Perissodactyla for zebras. Their most recent common ancestor is therefore the ancestor of the clade **Laurasiatheria**, which includes all modern carnivores, ungulates, bats, and a few other groups.

- **Laurasiatherian ancestor** – This ancestor lived roughly 90–100 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous/Early Paleocene. It gave rise to the major lineages that eventually led to carnivores (including lions) and odd‑toed ungulates (including zebras).

If you trace even further back, the last common ancestor of lions and zebras is simply the last common ancestor of **all placental mammals (Eutheria)**, which dates to about 160 million years ago. However, the most informative answer in terms of their evolutionary relationship is the Laurasiatherian ancestor.

So their last common ancestor would be the ancestor of Laurasiatheria. But if we go further back, the last common ancestor of all mammals is the ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria).
